name: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD)
capacity: 74 billion cubic meters reservoir; 6,450 MW hydroelectric — largest dam in Africa
downstream_impact: Egypt and Sudan face 12-25% reduction in Nile flow during filling. Egypt depends on Nile for 97% of freshwater. Sudan's Roseires and Merowe dams lose head pressure.
strategic_value: Gives Ethiopia control over Blue Nile flow (85% of total Nile water). Shifts hydro-hegemony from Egypt downstream to Ethiopia upstream. China financed turbines and electrical equipment.
alert: Egypt has repeatedly threatened military action. Fifth filling completed 2024. No binding trilateral agreement reached. Egypt classifies GERD as existential national security threat.

name: Aswan High Dam
controller: Egypt — Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation
capacity: Lake Nasser: 132 billion cubic meters; 2,100 MW hydroelectric
downstream_impact: Controls Egypt's entire agricultural and drinking water supply for 110 million people. Lake Nasser serves as strategic buffer against upstream disruption but loses 10 billion cubic meters/year to evaporation.
strategic_value: Built by Soviet Union 1960-1970, symbol of Cold War alliance. Now Egypt's last line of defense against GERD-driven flow reduction. Lake Nasser water levels are monitored as national security indicator.
alert: Lake Nasser dropped to concerning levels during GERD filling phases. If reservoir falls below 147m elevation, hydropower generation halts entirely.

name: Nile Basin Water Sharing Framework
capacity: 84 billion cubic meters total annual Nile flow shared among 11 nations, 500+ million people
downstream_impact: 1959 Egypt-Sudan treaty allocated 100% of Nile water to two countries. Upstream nations (Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, DRC, Eritrea, South Sudan) received zero allocation. Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) signed by 6 upstream states challenges Egypt's colonial-era water rights.
strategic_value: Control of Nile allocation determines food security for half a billion people. Framework collapse could trigger Africa's first inter-state water war.
alert: Egypt and Sudan refuse to sign CFA. Upstream bloc gaining diplomatic momentum. No enforceable international mechanism to resolve dispute.

name: Ataturk Dam (GAP Project)
capacity: 48.7 billion cubic meters reservoir; 2,400 MW hydroelectric. Part of GAP: 22 dams, 19 power plants across Euphrates-Tigris system
downstream_impact: Reduced Euphrates flow to Syria by 40% and to Iraq by up to 80% during peak impoundment. Iraq lost 70% of irrigated farmland in southern provinces. Syrian agriculture in Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor provinces collapsed.
strategic_value: Turkey's GAP project gives Ankara unilateral control over Euphrates-Tigris headwaters — water weapon over Syria and Iraq. NATO member controlling water supply of two conflict states.
alert: Iraq declared water emergency 2018-2023. No trilateral water-sharing treaty exists. Turkey uses flow control as political leverage.

name: Ilisu Dam
capacity: 10.4 billion cubic meters reservoir; 1,200 MW hydroelectric
downstream_impact: Reduced Tigris flow to Iraq by 56%. Iraq's southern marshlands — UNESCO World Heritage site — face total desiccation. Basra province drinking water contaminated with salt intrusion from reduced flow.
strategic_value: Completed 2020 despite European financier withdrawal over environmental and cultural concerns. Flooded ancient town of Hasankeyf (12,000 years of continuous habitation). Final link in Turkey's complete control of Tigris headwaters.
alert: Basra water crisis triggered mass protests 2018. Iraqi marshlands losing 50% of surface water. Salt levels in Shatt al-Arab waterway now exceed agricultural tolerance.

name: Tabqa Dam (al-Thawra Dam)
controller: CONTESTED — Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF/Kurdish) hold since 2017; Assad regime claims sovereignty
capacity: Lake Assad: 11.7 billion cubic meters; 824 MW hydroelectric
downstream_impact: During ISIS seizure (2014-2017), dam nearly catastrophically failed — would have flooded Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, and downstream Iraqi cities. Controls irrigation for 640,000 hectares of Syrian farmland.
strategic_value: Whoever holds Tabqa controls water and power for northern Syria. ISIS used dam as weapon, threatening to blow spillway. U.S.-backed SDF captured it in 2017. Turkey upstream controls inflow volume.
alert: Dam sustained structural damage during civil war battles. Engineering assessments warn of deterioration. A failure would be catastrophic for 3-4 million downstream residents.

name: Indus Waters Treaty
controller: CONTESTED — India issued notice to renegotiate Jan 2023; suspended treaty provisions post-Pulwama 2019
capacity: Indus system: 180 billion cubic meters annual flow. Treaty allocates 3 eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India, 3 western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan
downstream_impact: Pakistan depends on Indus system for 90% of agriculture — feeds 230 million people. India building Kishanganga and Ratle dams on western rivers, reducing Pakistan's allocation. Pakistan's Punjab and Sindh provinces face water stress.
strategic_value: World Bank-brokered 1960 treaty survived three wars — now collapsing. India's upstream position on all 6 rivers gives it theoretical capacity to weaponize water. Nuclear-armed states in water dispute.
alert: India formally moved to renegotiate treaty 2023. Kishanganga Dam operational since 2018 diverts Jhelum tributary. Pakistan calls it act of war. Two nuclear states, one river system, zero trust.

name: Kishanganga-Ratle Hydroelectric Complex
capacity: Kishanganga: 330 MW (operational 2018). Ratle: 850 MW (under construction). Combined reservoir capacity diverts Chenab and Jhelum tributaries.
downstream_impact: Pakistan claims projects violate Indus Waters Treaty by altering flow timing and volume of western rivers allocated to Pakistan. Reduces dry-season flow to Pakistan's breadbasket Punjab by an estimated 15-20%.
strategic_value: India building dams in contested Kashmir — projects serve dual purpose of power generation and demonstrating sovereignty over disputed territory. Pakistan initiated World Bank arbitration; India rejected jurisdiction.
alert: Construction accelerated post-2019 Kashmir autonomy revocation. Pakistan views as casus belli. World Bank arbitration process collapsed — no neutral arbiter remaining.

name: Rogun Dam
controller: Tajikistan — Barqi Tojik (state power company); partially financed by World Bank and Italian contractors
capacity: 335m height (world's tallest dam when complete); 13.3 billion cubic meters reservoir; 3,600 MW hydroelectric
downstream_impact: Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan face severe reduction in Amu Darya flow for cotton irrigation — Uzbekistan's primary export crop. Could reduce downstream flow by 15-20% during filling period of 13-16 years.
strategic_value: Shifts Central Asian hydro-power from downstream Uzbekistan to upstream Tajikistan. Russia mediates but benefits from regional dependency. China invested in Tajik infrastructure as BRI corridor leverage.
alert: First turbine operational 2018; dam only 60% complete. Uzbekistan threatened military action under Karimov. Relations improved under Mirziyoyev but structural tension remains. Seismic zone adds catastrophic failure risk.

name: Aral Sea Collapse Zone
controller: NO CONTROLLER — Soviet-era agricultural diversion destroyed 4th largest lake on Earth
capacity: LOST: was 68,000 sq km in 1960, now less than 10% remains. Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers diverted for cotton monoculture.
downstream_impact: Exposed seabed creates toxic dust storms carrying pesticides and salt across 500km radius. Regional cancer and respiratory disease rates 10-30x higher. Fishing industry (60,000 jobs) destroyed. Local climate altered — hotter summers, colder winters.
strategic_value: Worst environmental disaster in modern history. Kazakhstan's Kok-Aral Dam (2005, World Bank-funded) partially restored North Aral Sea, but South Aral is unrecoverable. Cautionary tale for every water dispute on this board.
alert: South Aral Sea effectively dead. Toxic dust storms reach as far as Antarctic ice cores. Uzbekistan continues cotton irrigation that caused the collapse. No political will to reduce diversion.

name: Lancang-Mekong Dam Cascade
controller: China — Huaneng Lancang River Hydropower Inc. (state-owned)
capacity: 11 mega-dams on upper Mekong (Lancang) with 42 billion cubic meters total storage; 21,300 MW combined hydroelectric capacity. Nuozhadu alone: 22.4 billion cubic meters.
downstream_impact: Controls 50% of Mekong dry-season flow to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam. Downstream fisheries collapsed — 60 million people depend on Mekong fish protein. Tonle Sap lake in Cambodia shrinking. Vietnam's Mekong Delta facing saltwater intrusion destroying rice production.
strategic_value: China controls the tap for 6 downstream nations. Uses water release timing as diplomatic leverage — withheld data during 2019-2020 downstream drought. Mekong is BRI's water dimension: infrastructure debt + water dependency = total leverage.
tag: CHINA'S WATER WEAPON OVER SOUTHEAST ASIA
alert: Mekong River Commission has no enforcement power over China. U.S. launched Mekong-U.S. Partnership to counter. Downstream nations have zero ability to compel water release. Satellite data proved China held water during 2020 drought while claiming normal flow.

name: Jordan River Basin
controller: Israel — controls all major tributaries (Yarmouk partially shared with Jordan), National Water Carrier diverts from Sea of Galilee
capacity: CRITICALLY DEPLETED: 1.3 billion cubic meters historical annual flow reduced to less than 100 million reaching Dead Sea. Dead Sea dropping 1 meter/year.
downstream_impact: Palestinians in West Bank receive 1/4 the per-capita water of Israeli settlers from shared aquifers. Jordan receives fixed allocation under 1994 peace treaty but faces 40% water deficit. Gaza's aquifer 97% undrinkable from contamination and over-extraction.
strategic_value: Water control is inseparable from territorial control in Israel-Palestine conflict. Israel's desalination capacity (now 80% of domestic supply) reduced dependency on Jordan River but maintains control of West Bank aquifers as leverage.
alert: Dead Sea on track to disappear by 2050. Red Sea-Dead Sea canal project repeatedly stalled. Gaza water crisis classified as humanitarian emergency by UN. 2.3 million people with near-zero clean water access.

name: Great Man-Made River (GMMR)
controller: DAMAGED — No unified controller since 2011. Libya's rival governments both claim authority. Infrastructure deteriorating without maintenance.
capacity: World's largest irrigation project: 2,820 km pipeline, 6.5 million cubic meters/day from Nubian Sandstone Aquifer. $25 billion Gaddafi-era investment (1984-2007).
downstream_impact: Supplied 70% of Libya's freshwater to Tripoli, Benghazi, Sirte. Damage from civil war (NATO bombing hit pipeline sections 2011, militia attacks ongoing) cut supply to millions. Tripoli faces recurring water shutoffs.
strategic_value: Draws from non-renewable fossil aquifer shared with Egypt, Chad, Sudan. Aquifer depletion irreversible — estimated 50-100 year supply remaining at design extraction rates. Civil war turned infrastructure into military target.
alert: Multiple pipeline sections damaged and unrepaired since 2011. Militia groups control pump stations as leverage. Fossil aquifer cannot recharge — every liter extracted is gone permanently. Population of 7 million depends on system with no maintenance budget.

name: South-North Water Transfer Project
controller: China — State Council South-North Water Transfer Project Construction Committee
capacity: Eastern and Central routes operational: 44.8 billion cubic meters annual transfer capacity. 2,899 km of canals. $80+ billion total investment — most expensive water project in history.
downstream_impact: Diverts Yangtze River water to arid north (Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei). Southern provinces face reduced Yangtze flow during droughts — 2022 Yangtze drought worst in 500 years exposed limits. Western route (from Tibetan plateau) would affect Mekong, Brahmaputra, and Salween headwaters — threatening India, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia.
strategic_value: Sustains water supply to China's political capital and northern industrial base. Planned Western Route from Tibetan Plateau would give China control over headwaters flowing to India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam — affecting 2 billion people.
tag: CHINA'S INTERNAL WATER REPLUMBING — GLOBAL CONSEQUENCES
alert: Western Route (not yet built) would divert Brahmaputra headwaters — India considers this a red line. If constructed, would affect water supply to 1.4 billion people in South and Southeast Asia. Yangtze source depletion accelerating from climate change.
